blocks.text: 1. Gaussian Mixture Models

blocks.alt: Multiple Gaussian distributions mix together into a GMM

blocks.text: K-Means, DBSCAN, and Mean Shift, the three clustering algorithms covered so far in this module, all share one trait in common: every data point ends up assigned to exactly one cluster, a hard, all-or-nothing assignment. Gaussian Mixture Models, GMM for short, take a genuinely different, fully probabilistic view. Instead of forcing a single definitive answer, GMM assigns every point a probability of belonging to each cluster, a soft assignment that can express genuine uncertainty about which group a point really belongs to.

This directly echoes the Gaussian variant of Naive Bayes, covered in the Classification module, which modeled each feature as normally distributed within a known class. GMM applies essentially the same Gaussian, bell-shaped distribution modeling idea, but for a fully unsupervised problem, where the class, or cluster, that generated each point is not known at all and must be inferred purely from the data's structure.
2. The Mixture Idea

blocks.alt: Cluster 1 and cluster 2, each a Gaussian, combine into a weighted mixture

blocks.text: GMM starts from a specific generative assumption about how the data came to exist: it assumes the observed data was actually produced by a mixture of several separate Gaussian, bell-shaped, probability distributions, each one representing a genuine underlying cluster. Every one of these Gaussian components has its own mean, marking its center, and its own spread and orientation, describing how that component's points are scattered around that center.

Under this assumption, every individual data point was drawn from exactly one of these underlying Gaussian components, but which specific component produced any particular point is not directly observed, only the final data point itself is. GMM's entire task is to work backward from the observed data alone: simultaneously estimate the parameters, mean and spread, of every Gaussian component, and estimate the probability that each individual data point originated from each of those components.
3. Soft Assignment versus Hard Assignment

blocks.alt: K-Means gives hard assignment while GMM gives soft assignment

blocks.text: The practical difference between GMM's soft assignment and K-Means' hard assignment matters most exactly where clusters are not cleanly separated. K-Means declares a point belongs to precisely one cluster, full stop, regardless of how close that point might actually sit to the boundary with a neighboring cluster. GMM instead reports something like a 70 percent probability of belonging to cluster A and a 30 percent probability of belonging to cluster B for a point sitting in an ambiguous, overlapping region between the two.

When clusters in the data truly are well separated, with clear gaps between them, hard and soft assignment tend to agree almost completely, and K-Means' simpler, faster approach works perfectly well. When clusters genuinely overlap, however, which is common in real data, GMM's soft assignment captures a kind of honest uncertainty that K-Means simply cannot express, since K-Means is mathematically incapable of reporting anything other than a single definitive cluster label for every point.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: GMM can still produce a hard clustering if needed, simply by assigning each point to whichever component has the highest probability for it. The soft probabilities remain available underneath, useful whenever that extra uncertainty information matters for a downstream decision.

blocks.text: 4. Fitting with the EM Algorithm

blocks.alt: An E-step estimating assignments and an M-step updating parameters repeat until converged

blocks.text: GMM is fit using the Expectation-Maximization algorithm, EM for short, a two-step iterative loop that closely parallels the assign-then-recompute loop already covered for K-Means, but adapted to work with probabilities rather than hard assignments. Starting from a rough initial guess for every component's mean and spread, the E-step, Expectation, computes the probability that each data point belongs to each component, given the current parameter estimates.

The M-step, Maximization, then updates every component's mean and spread, using the probabilities just computed in the E-step as weights, so points more likely to belong to a given component have proportionally more influence on that component's updated parameters. These two steps alternate, E-step then M-step then E-step again, each round refining the component parameters and the point probabilities together, until the parameters stop changing meaningfully between rounds, at which point the algorithm has converged.

blocks.text: 5. Capturing Cluster Shape with Covariance

K-Means centroids capture only a single location, the mean position of a cluster, with no information at all about that cluster's shape, size, or orientation. GMM components carry substantially more information: alongside a mean, each component also has a covariance, a mathematical description of how spread out, and in what direction, the points belonging to that component tend to scatter.

Different covariance structures offer different tradeoffs between flexibility and simplicity. A spherical covariance constrains every component to be a perfectly circular, or spherical in higher dimensions, cluster, closest in spirit to K-Means' implicit assumption. A diagonal covariance allows elliptical clusters, but only ones aligned with the original feature axes. A full covariance allows elliptical clusters at any orientation at all, the most flexible and expressive option, at the cost of more parameters to estimate.

blocks.text: 6. Fitting Elliptical Clusters

blocks.alt: K-Means only fits round clusters while GMM fits elliptical clusters

blocks.text: K-Means, relying purely on distance to a single centroid, implicitly forces every cluster boundary to be roughly circular, or spherical in higher dimensions, an assumption already flagged as a real limitation back in the K-Means topic. GMM with full covariance components removes this constraint entirely, capable of fitting clusters that are elongated, tilted at an angle, or otherwise genuinely elliptical in shape, matching the natural structure of real data far more often than a strict circular assumption allows.

This is a genuinely different kind of flexibility than the shape flexibility DBSCAN and Mean Shift offer through density connectivity; GMM's elliptical flexibility comes from its explicit, parametric Gaussian shape assumption instead, which makes it well suited whenever clusters plausibly follow a smooth, unimodal, bell-shaped spread, even if that spread happens to be stretched or tilted, rather than the more irregular, potentially non-convex shapes DBSCAN handles.
7. GMM as Maximum Likelihood Estimation

blocks.alt: Data feeds maximum likelihood to find the best parameters

blocks.text: It is worth connecting GMM's fitting process back to Maximum Likelihood Estimation, already covered in depth for Logistic Regression's coefficient fitting. GMM fitting is, at its core, also an instance of Maximum Likelihood Estimation: the goal is to find whichever set of component means, spreads, and mixing proportions makes the observed data, as a whole, most probable under the assumed mixture-of-Gaussians model.

The complication, compared to Logistic Regression's more direct MLE via gradient-based optimization, is that the true origin component of each data point is never actually observed, only its final feature values are. The EM algorithm is precisely the standard technique for carrying out Maximum Likelihood Estimation in exactly this kind of situation, where some relevant information, here, which component generated each point, is missing or hidden, alternating between estimating that missing information, the E-step, and updating the model parameters given that estimate, the M-step.
8. Choosing the Number of Components

blocks.alt: Trying many component counts under BIC or AIC chooses the best count

blocks.text: Like K-Means, GMM requires the number of components, effectively the number of clusters, to be chosen before fitting begins, and choosing this well matters just as much here as choosing K did for K-Means. Rather than relying on the Elbow Method, GMM offers a more principled alternative rooted directly in its probabilistic foundation: information criteria such as the Bayesian Information Criterion, BIC, and the Akaike Information Criterion, AIC.

Both BIC and AIC balance how well a fitted model explains the observed data against how many parameters that model required to achieve that fit, penalizing models that are needlessly complex relative to how much they actually improve the fit. The standard practical approach is to fit GMM across a range of candidate component counts and select whichever count minimizes BIC, or alternatively AIC, giving a genuinely more statistically grounded way to choose the number of clusters than the visual, somewhat subjective elbow-spotting the Elbow Method relies on.

blocks.title: tip
blocks.content: BIC penalizes model complexity more heavily than AIC does, which tends to make BIC favor a simpler model with fewer components. When the two criteria disagree on the best number of components, that disagreement itself is often a useful signal that the right number is genuinely ambiguous given the available data.

blocks.text: 9. Worked Example
The example below fits a Gaussian Mixture Model with full covariance, compares BIC across a few candidate component counts, and inspects the soft probability assignments directly.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Two overlapping groups of customers by annual spend (thousands) and visit frequency
X = np.array([
    [2, 1], [3, 2], [2.5, 1.5], [4, 2.5], [3.5, 2],
    [15, 8], [16, 9], [14.5, 7.5], [13, 7], [14, 7.8],
])

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

# Compare BIC across a few candidate numbers of components
for n_components in [1, 2, 3, 4]:
    model = GaussianMixture(n_components=n_components, covariance_type='full', random_state=42)
    model.fit(X_scaled)
    print(f"n_components={n_components}: BIC={model.bic(X_scaled):.2f}")

# Fit the chosen number of components and inspect soft assignments
final_model = GaussianMixture(n_components=2, covariance_type='full', random_state=42)
final_model.fit(X_scaled)

hard_labels = final_model.predict(X_scaled)
soft_probabilities = final_model.predict_proba(X_scaled)

print("Hard cluster labels:", hard_labels)
print("Soft probabilities for the first three points:")
print(np.round(soft_probabilities[:3], 3))

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: predict_proba returns, for every point, its probability of belonging to each component, summing to 1 across components. A point with probabilities close to 0.5 and 0.5 sits right in the ambiguous zone between two clusters, exactly the kind of case hard assignment methods like K-Means cannot express.

blocks.text: 10. Key Takeaways

items: Gaussian Mixture Models assign every point a probability of belonging to each cluster, a soft assignment rather than a hard one.
GMM assumes the data was generated by a mixture of Gaussian components, each with its own mean and covariance.
Fitting uses the EM algorithm: alternating an E-step (compute point probabilities) and an M-step (update component parameters).
Covariance type, spherical, diagonal, or full, controls how much cluster shape flexibility the model allows.
Full covariance GMM can fit elongated, tilted elliptical clusters that K-Means's spherical assumption cannot represent.
GMM fitting is Maximum Likelihood Estimation, carried out via EM because the true cluster origin of each point is hidden.
BIC and AIC give a principled, complexity-penalized way to choose the number of components, an alternative to the Elbow Method.
Soft probabilities are especially valuable whenever clusters genuinely overlap and hard boundaries would misrepresent real ambiguity.
Next up: Spectral Clustering, a graph-based method that handles non-convex cluster shapes GMM's Gaussian assumption still cannot capture.
